title: The next-word detective
objectives: Explain next-token prediction using a familiar sentence.
Distinguish a likely continuation from a verified fact.
prediction: Finish this sentence before reading further: I drink a cup of ___. Would tea, socks, or moon be a more ordinary continuation?
explanation: You probably picked tea. You have seen many examples of cups and drinks, so that continuation fits. A language model also uses patterns learned from examples to assign probabilities to possible next pieces of text.

LLM means large language model. In many text-generation systems, the model predicts a next token, the application selects one, and the process repeats. A token is a text piece; for now we use whole words to keep the idea visible.

A model can assign high probability to a familiar claim even when the claim is false. Likely wording is not a fact check. We will later add source notes and evaluations to make our chatbot more dependable.

Start with a Python dictionary. A dictionary stores key-value pairs. Our hand-written table can map a sentence prefix to one next word. This is a rule table, not a trained LLM, but you can inspect its entire behavior.
analogy_limit: The detective analogy describes finding a plausible continuation. Real LLMs do not consult our tiny dictionary and do not guarantee truth. Their token choices depend on learned numerical parameters and the supplied context.

python_example.code:
next_word = {
    'I drink a cup of': 'tea',
    'The cat says': 'meow',
}
prompt = 'I drink a cup of'
print(next_word.get(prompt, 'I do not know yet'))
print(next_word.get('The rocket likes', 'I do not know yet'))
python_example.expected_output:
tea
I do not know yet
walkthrough: The dictionary key is a known prefix; its value is our chosen next word.
get(key, default) returns the value when the key exists, otherwise the default.
The second prefix is missing, so the fallback is printed rather than inventing an entry.

game.title: Next Word Detective
game.instructions: Choose the most ordinary continuation for each scene. These answers describe common language patterns, not laws about the world. Get two of three right to pass.

rounds.prompt: The sky is full of dark clouds. It might ___ soon.

feedback.a: Rain is a familiar continuation. It is a prediction, not a weather report.
feedback.b: Sandwich is a noun that does not fit this ordinary verb slot.
feedback.c: Keyboard does not describe the ordinary event suggested by the clouds.

rounds.prompt: I used a spoon to eat the ___.

feedback.a: A bicycle is not an ordinary food. A silly story could use it, but that is not this task.
feedback.c: Thunder is a sound, so it is not an ordinary thing to eat.

rounds.prompt: A fluent chatbot says our fictional town was founded in 1620. No source was provided. What have we established?

choices.text: It produced a plausible sentence; we still need evidence
The model looked at the town archives

feedback.b: We have no evidence of an archive lookup or tool call.
feedback.c: Exactly. The sentence may sound right without being supported.

questions.prompt: What is the simplified repeating step in text generation?

choices.text: Retrain the model after every word

feedback.a: The selected token becomes part of the context for the next step.
feedback.b: Web search requires a separate connected tool; generation alone does not imply it.
feedback.c: Normal inference does not retrain the model after each token.

questions.prompt: Is the example dictionary a trained LLM?

choices.text: No, it is a hand-authored lookup toy

feedback.a: Printing text is not enough to make a system an LLM.
feedback.b: You wrote the entries directly. Nothing learned parameters from data here.
feedback.c: A programming language does not determine whether a model learned from data.

questions.prompt: Why should an important factual answer be checked?

choices.text: Because short replies are always wrong
Because plausible wording can be unsupported

feedback.b: Python can store factual data; that is unrelated to the model's claim.
feedback.c: Prediction can produce an unsupported claim. Evidence and evaluation help.

build.title: Add one prediction and one honest fallback
build.instructions: Copy the example into a local Python file. Add the prefix 'My robot likes' with the continuation 'puzzles'. Print that result and the result for one prefix you did not add.
criteria: The new known prefix prints puzzles.
The unknown prefix prints the fallback rather than raising an error.
hints: Add another key-value pair inside the dictionary.
Use .get() with the same fallback for both lookups.

reflection: Explain to a friend why a chatbot can sound confident without proving its answer is true.
tutor_context: Basic Python dictionary learner. Explain likely next text versus verified truth. Keep whole-word prediction explicitly labeled as a simplification; give hints before the mission solution.
